mstts:express-as.prosody: Let’s talk about something we’ve all heard before—especially if you’re a woman: Chapter Six, “The Myth of Having It All.” There’s this story that gets told, right? If you just try hard enough, plan well enough, push yourself far enough—you’ll be able to have it all. The dream job. The loving family. A buzzing social life, a fit and healthy body, a life full of meaning. But if you’re anything like most people, you know life doesn’t really work that way. In reality, things are a lot messier. Chasing after “having it all” can turn into a trap of its own. Picture this: there’s a woman who’s always felt the pressure to balance everything. Some days, it was like she was juggling a dozen fragile plates—work deadlines, family dinners, friendships, exercise, self-care—and any second now, one of those plates might come crashing down. She’d scroll through social media, seeing everyone else’s perfect smiles and color-coded calendars, and think, “Clearly, they’ve figured it out. Why can’t I?” But behind those pretty pictures, the truth was different. There were birthdays she missed, emails left unanswered, nights spent lying awake worrying about disappointing someone. And the guilt? It was always close by. Guilt for not being present enough at home. Or not crushing it at work. Or not reaching out to friends. Or not taking better care of herself. Most people don’t talk about the trade-offs—the things that quietly slip through the cracks when you’re spread thin. Over time, though, something started to shift. She realized that “having it all” wasn’t about getting everything perfect. It was about making choices. Some chapters of life called for more focus at work. Others needed more energy at home, or for health, or for relationships. There’s no magic formula—no way to do everything at once. The real challenge? Letting go of the myth. Accepting that it’s okay to drop a plate sometimes. Forgiving yourself for being—well, human. And here’s something important: those true moments of happiness didn’t come from reaching some impossible standard. They showed up in the small, imperfect moments—a late-night talk with a friend, a peaceful walk after a long day, a project finished not perfectly, but with heart. So, if you ever catch yourself chasing after the idea of “having it all,” remember—maybe the secret is to redefine what “all” really means to you.
